title: String Tricks
blurb: The handful of text methods you'll use every day: trim, case, includes, slice, split and padStart.
intro:
Names, messages, search boxes, file names: most data is text. These five stages cover the string tools that do 90% of the work.

Five quick stages, about five minutes.

stages.l:
Text typed by people is messy: extra spaces, random capitals. Two methods fix most of it:

console.log("  Hello  ".trim());
console.log("Hello".toUpperCase());
console.log("Hello".toLowerCase());
Hello
HELLO
hello

String methods never change the original text. They give you a new string back. You can also chain them: s.trim().toUpperCase().
stages.p: Write clean(s) that returns s with the spaces cut off both ends and every letter in lowercase.
stages.h: Chain two of the methods from the example and return the result.

stages.l: slice(start, end) copies part of a string. It starts at start and stops just before end. Negative numbers count from the end.
stages.p: What does this print?
miss: slice copies letters exactly as they are, capital S included.
slice stops just before index 4, so it's only 4 letters.
slice(0, 4) takes indexes 0, 1, 2 and 3: four letters. And -6 means the last six.
stages.why: Indexes 0 to 3 are Java. slice(-6) starts 6 from the end and goes to the end: Script.
stages.h: Count the letters: J is 0, a is 1, v is 2, a is 3, S is 4.

stages.l:
includes checks whether one string is inside another. startsWith and endsWith check the ends.

console.log("photo.png".endsWith(".png"));
console.log("Hello world".includes("lo w"));
true
true
stages.p: Write hasBadWord(message, bad). bad is an array of words. Return true if the message contains any of them, ignoring capitals.
stages.h: Lowercase the message once, then use bad.some(w => ...) with includes.

stages.l:
split breaks text into an array at a separator. join glues an array back into text.

const parts = "red,green,blue".split(",");
console.log(parts);
console.log(parts.join(" + "));
["red", "green", "blue"]
red + green + blue
stages.p: Write initials(fullName) that returns the first letter of each word, in capitals, with no spaces. "ada lovelace" gives "AL".
stages.h: Split on " ", map each word to w[0].toUpperCase(), then join("").

stages.l:
padStart(length, fill) and padEnd(length, fill) add characters until a string is long enough. They're how scoreboards line up.

console.log("7".padStart(3, "0"));
console.log("ab".padEnd(5, ".") + "|");
007
ab...|
stages.p: Write row(name, score) for a scoreboard: the name padded with dots on the right to 10 characters, then the score padded with spaces on the left to 5 characters.
stages.h: name.padEnd(10, ".") + String(score).padStart(5, " ").

title: Array One-Liners
blurb: Do in one line what used to take a whole loop: map, filter, find, some and reduce.
intro:
Arrays come with built-in tools that each do one common loop job. Learn to spot which one you need and your code gets much shorter.

Five quick stages, about five minutes.

stages.l:
map runs a function on every item and gives back a new array of the results, the same length as before.

const names = ["kit", "robin"];
console.log(names.map(n => n.toUpperCase()));
["KIT", "ROBIN"]
stages.p: Write prices(items). Each item is { name, price }. Return an array of just the prices.
stages.h: items.map(it => it.price).

stages.l:
Pick the right tool

map: change every item. filter: keep some items. find: get the first match. some / every: yes-or-no questions. reduce: boil everything down to one value.
stages.p: You have an array of players and want to know: is anyone still alive?
stages.q: Which method answers that in one line?
miss: map gives back a whole new array, not a yes or no.
filter gives a list of the alive players. That works, but you'd still need .length > 0.
reduce could do it, but it's the long way round.
stages.why: some returns true as soon as one item passes the test. It's the direct answer to "is anyone...?"
stages.h: The question has a yes or no answer.

stages.l:
filter keeps the items where your test returns true.

console.log([3, -1, 8, 0].filter(n => n > 0));
[3, 8]
stages.p: Write passed(scores) that returns only the scores of 50 or more.
stages.h: Test with s >= 50.

stages.l:
find returns the first item that passes the test, or undefined if none do. Use ?? to give a fallback.

const pets = [{ kind: "cat" }, { kind: "dog" }];
console.log(pets.find(p => p.kind === "fish") ?? "no fish");
no fish
stages.p: Write byId(users, id) that returns the user's name, or "Unknown" if no user has that id.
stages.h: Find the user, then use ?.name ?? "Unknown".

stages.l:
The tools chain together. Each step's result flows into the next.

const words = ["hi", "hello", "hey"];
console.log(words.filter(w => w.length > 2).map(w => w.length).reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0));
8
stages.p: Write bestTotal(orders). Each order is { paid, amount }. Add up the amount of only the paid orders.
stages.h: filter by o.paid, map to o.amount, reduce with a start of 0.

title: Random Picks
blurb: Dice rolls, coin flips, random picks from a list and chance-based events with Math.random.
intro:
Games, quizzes and name pickers all need randomness. It all comes from one function, Math.random(), plus a little maths.

Five quick stages, about five minutes.

stages.t: A whole number in a range
stages.l:
Math.random() gives a decimal from 0 up to (but never) 1. To get a whole number from min to max:

// a dice roll: 1 to 6
const roll = Math.floor(Math.random() * 6) + 1;

Times 6 gives 0 to 5.99…, floor gives 0 to 5, and + 1 shifts it to 1 to 6. In general it's times how many numbers there are, then plus the smallest.

Testing random code

Here, the random number is passed in as r, so the checker can test exact values. In real code you'd use Math.random() in its place.
stages.p: Write between(min, max, r) that turns r (from 0 up to 1) into a whole number from min to max, including both.
stages.h: There are max - min + 1 numbers. Math.floor(r * (max - min + 1)) + min.

stages.l: The most common random bug is forgetting the + 1 or putting it in the wrong place.
stages.p:
This is meant to roll a dice:

const roll = Math.floor(Math.random() * 6);
stages.q: Which numbers can it actually produce?
miss: There's no + 1, so it never shifts up to start at 1.
Math.random() never reaches 1, so times 6 never reaches 6.
Without + 1 it starts at 0, and it can reach 5.
stages.why: Without + 1 you get 0 to 5: a 0 instead of a 6. The fix is Math.floor(Math.random() * 6) + 1.
stages.h: What's the smallest and largest value of Math.random() * 6, rounded down?

stages.l:
To pick a random item, pick a random index from 0 to length - 1.

const colors = ["red", "green", "blue"];
const i = Math.floor(Math.random() * colors.length);
stages.p: Write pick(list, r) that uses r to choose and return a random item from list.
stages.h: list[Math.floor(r * list.length)].

stages.l:
Something that should happen 30% of the time: check whether the random number is below 0.3.

if (Math.random() < 0.5) console.log("Heads");
else console.log("Tails");
stages.p: Write chance(percent, r) that returns true when r falls inside the chance. chance(30, 0.2) is true and chance(30, 0.5) is false.
stages.h: Turn the percent into a decimal by dividing by 100, then compare with <.

stages.l:
Putting it together: random choices can drive any decision.

const coin = r => (r < 0.5 ? "heads" : "tails");
console.log([0.1, 0.7].map(coin));
["heads", "tails"]
stages.p: Write teams(names, rolls). rolls[i] is the random number for names[i]. Below 0.5 goes to team red, otherwise blue. Return { red: [...], blue: [...] }.
stages.h: Start with { red: [], blue: [] } and loop with forEach((n, i) => ...), pushing into the right team.

title: Dates and Times
blurb: Make dates, read the parts, count days between them and write them out neatly.
intro:
Birthdays, deadlines, streaks and timers all need dates. JavaScript's Date has a few odd habits, and this module covers the ones that trip everyone up.

Five quick stages, about five minutes.

stages.l:
A Date holds one moment in time. Make one from numbers, then read the pieces with get methods:

const d = new Date(2030, 0, 15);   // 15 January 2030
console.log(d.getFullYear(), d.getMonth(), d.getDate(), d.getDay());
2030 0 15 2

The odd one: months count from 0, so January is 0 and December is 11. getDay() is the day of the week, where 0 is Sunday, 1 is Monday and so on.
stages.p: Write weekday(year, month, day), where month is a normal month number (January is 1). Return the day of the week as a word, like "Tuesday".
stages.h: Make the date with month - 1. Keep a list of day names starting with "Sunday" and use getDay() as the index.

stages.l: Because months start at 0, the month number you type is one more than you might think.
stages.p: What does this print?
miss: 3 isn't March here: months count from 0, so 0 is January.
getMonth() gives back exactly the 3 that was put in.
Index 3 exists in the list.
stages.why: Month 3 is the fourth month, April. getMonth() returns 3, and index 3 in the list is "Apr", because the list counts from 0 too.
stages.h: 0 is January, 1 is February...

stages.l:
Inside, a date is a count of milliseconds since 1 January 1970. Subtracting two dates gives the milliseconds between them. Dates can also be made from text written year-month-day:

const ms = new Date("2030-01-02") - new Date("2030-01-01");
console.log(ms);              // milliseconds in one day
console.log(ms / 1000 / 60);  // in minutes
86400000
1440
stages.p: Write daysBetween(from, to). Both are text like "2030-01-31". Return how many days it is from from to to, rounded to the nearest day.
stages.h: A day is 1000 * 60 * 60 * 24 milliseconds. Turn both into dates, subtract, divide by a day and Math.round.

stages.l:
Computers like dates written year-month-day (called ISO format), like 2030-01-05, because they sort correctly as text. Pad single digits with a 0:

const n = 7;
console.log(String(n).padStart(2, "0"));
07
stages.p: Write isoDate(year, month, day) that returns the date as YYYY-MM-DD, with the month and day always 2 digits.
stages.h: Pad month and day to 2 characters, then join the three parts with "-".

stages.l:
Dates compare with < and >, and JavaScript fixes overflow for you: day 32 of January becomes 1 February.

const d = new Date(2030, 0, 32);
console.log(d.getMonth() + 1, d.getDate());
2 1
stages.p: Write untilBirthday(today, month, day). today is text like "2030-05-20" and the birthday month is 1 to 12. Return how many days until the next birthday: 0 if it's today, and next year's if it already passed this year.
stages.h: Make now = new Date(today), then new Date(isoText) for this year's birthday using the isoDate idea, so both dates are made the same way. If it's before now, use next year. Then use the days-between maths.

title: Object Shortcuts
blurb: Modern ways to build, copy, merge and unpack objects in less code.
intro:
Objects are everywhere in JavaScript. A few modern shortcuts make working with them faster and safer.

Five quick stages, about five minutes.

stages.l:
When a property has the same name as the variable holding its value, you can write it once:

const x = 3, y = 4;
const point = { x, y };   // same as { x: x, y: y }
console.log(point);
{ x: 3, y: 4 }
stages.p: Write makeUser(name, age) that returns an object with name, age and active: true, using shorthand for name and age.
stages.h: return { name, age, active: true };

stages.l: The spread ... copies all of an object's properties into a new one. Properties written after it win.
stages.p: What does this print?
miss: The spread made a copy, so base wasn't changed.
speed: 5 comes after the spread, so it replaces the copied 2.
hp was copied over by the spread.
stages.why: fast is a brand new object: it copies hp: 10 and speed: 2, then speed: 5 overwrites the copy. base is untouched.
stages.h: Spread first copies, then later properties overwrite.

stages.l:
Spread is the classic way to fill in default settings: spread the defaults first, then the user's choices on top.

const merged = { ...{ a: 1, b: 2 }, ...{ b: 9 } };
console.log(merged);
{ a: 1, b: 9 }
stages.p: Write withDefaults(options) that returns the defaults { sound: true, volume: 50, theme: "light" } with anything in options replacing them.
stages.h: return { sound: true, volume: 50, theme: "light", ...options };

stages.l:
Destructuring pulls properties out into variables in one line. You can give defaults too.

const pet = { kind: "cat", name: "Tom" };
const { kind, legs = 4 } = pet;
console.log(kind, legs);
cat 4
stages.p: Write label(item) using destructuring to get name and qty (default 1), and return "3 × apples" style text.
stages.h: const { name, qty = 1 } = item; then return qty + " × " + name.

stages.t: Quick challenge: loop over an object
stages.l:
Object.entries turns an object into [key, value] pairs you can loop over and destructure.

for (const [k, v] of Object.entries({ a: 1, b: 2 })) console.log(k + "=" + v);
a=1
b=2
stages.p: Write describe(stats) that returns text like "hp: 10, mp: 4", one key: value per property, joined with ", ".
stages.h: Object.entries(stats).map(([k, v]) => k + ": " + v).join(", ").

title: Unique Values with Sets
blurb: Remove duplicates, check membership fast and compare lists with Set.
intro:
A Set is a collection where every value appears at most once. That one rule makes a lot of jobs easy.

Five quick stages, about five minutes.

stages.l:
Put a list into a Set and the duplicates disappear. Spread it back into an array with [...set].

const s = new Set(["a", "b", "a"]);
console.log(s.size);
console.log([...s]);
2
["a", "b"]
stages.p: Write unique(list) that returns a new array with duplicates removed, in the order they first appeared.
stages.h: One line: spread a new Set made from the list.

stages.l: Sets have their own methods: add, has, delete and the size property. Adding something that's already there does nothing.
stages.p: What does this print?
miss: The second "cat" wasn't added again, and dog was deleted.
Sets never hold the same value twice.
cat was added and never deleted.
stages.why: The Set holds cat and dog (the second cat is ignored), then dog is deleted. One item is left: cat.
stages.h: Track the Set after each line.

stages.l:
has on a Set is very fast, even with millions of items. That makes it perfect for "have I seen this before?" questions.

const visited = new Set();
visited.add("room1");
if (!visited.has("room2")) console.log("New room!");
New room!
stages.p: Write firstRepeat(list) that returns the first value that appears for a second time, or null if nothing repeats.
stages.h: Loop through the list. If the Set already has the value, return it. Otherwise add it. After the loop, return null.

stages.l:
To find what two lists share, turn one into a Set, then filter the other.

const vowels = new Set("aeiou");
console.log([..."hello"].filter(ch => vowels.has(ch)));
["e", "o"]
stages.p: Write common(a, b) that returns the items of a that are also in b, without duplicates, in a's order.
stages.h: Make new Set(b), filter a with has, then remove duplicates like the first stage.

stages.l:
Sets answer "who's missing?" just as easily: keep the items that the Set does not have.

const done = new Set(["maths"]);
console.log(["maths", "art"].filter(s => !done.has(s)));
["art"]
stages.p: Write absent(roster, present) that returns everyone on the roster who isn't in the present list.
stages.h: Make a Set of present, then filter the roster with !here.has(name).

title: Rounding Numbers
blurb: Round, floor, ceil, decimals, percents and keeping numbers inside limits.
intro:
Numbers that look right matter: 33% not 33.33333%, $4.50 not $4.5, and a volume that never goes past 100.

Five quick stages, about five minutes.

stages.l:
Math.round goes to the nearest whole number, Math.floor always goes down and Math.ceil always goes up.

console.log(Math.round(2.5), Math.floor(2.9), Math.ceil(2.1));
3 2 3

Use ceil when a part still needs a whole thing: 21 people in 4-seat cars still need 6 cars.
stages.p: Write pages(items, perPage) that returns how many pages you need to show all the items.
stages.h: Divide and round up.

stages.l: toFixed(n) rounds to n decimal places, but it returns a string, not a number.
stages.p: What does this print?
miss: toFixed always returns a string.
toFixed(2) keeps two decimals: 4.50.
+ with a string glues text on instead of adding.
stages.why: "4.50" + 1 is string gluing, so you get "4.501". Use toFixed only at the very end, for display.
stages.h: What type does toFixed return, and what does + do with text?

stages.l:
To round to decimal places and keep a number, multiply, round, then divide.

console.log(Math.round(3.14159 * 10) / 10);
3.1
stages.p: Write roundTo(n, places) that rounds n to places decimal places and returns a number.
stages.h: The multiplier is 10 ** places.

stages.l:
Clamping keeps a number between a minimum and a maximum: volume from 0 to 100, health from 0 to max.

console.log(Math.min(120, 100));   // the smaller one
console.log(Math.max(-5, 0));      // the bigger one
100
0
stages.p: Write clamp(n, min, max) that returns n, but never less than min or more than max.
stages.h: Combine both: Math.min(Math.max(n, min), max).

stages.l:
Percent is part divided by whole, times 100. Always guard against dividing by 0.

console.log(Math.round(1 / 3 * 100) + "%");
33%
stages.p: Write percent(part, whole) that returns a label like "33%", rounded to a whole number. If whole is 0, return "0%".
stages.h: Check for 0 first, then Math.round(part / whole * 100) + "%".

title: Counting Things
blurb: Tally votes, letters and words with an object, then find the most common one.
intro:
"How many of each?" is one of the most useful questions in programming: votes, inventory, word counts, high scores. One small pattern answers it.

Five quick stages, about five minutes.

stages.l:
Keep an object with one key per thing. For each item, add 1 to its key, starting from 0 the first time.

const count = {};
for (const fruit of ["apple", "pear", "apple"]) {
  count[fruit] = (count[fruit] || 0) + 1;
}
console.log(count);
{ apple: 2, pear: 1 }
stages.p: Write tally(votes) that returns an object counting how many votes each option got.
stages.h: The same loop as the example, with votes.

stages.l: Reading a key that doesn't exist yet gives undefined. And undefined + 1 is not a number.
stages.p: What does this print?
miss: count.cat starts as undefined, not 0.
undefined + 1 is a number, but a broken one.
Nothing set count.cat to 0 first.
stages.why: undefined + 1 is NaN (Not a Number). || 0 swaps the missing undefined for 0, so the count starts properly.
stages.h: What is undefined + 1?

stages.l:
Strings can be looped over letter by letter with for...of, so the tally pattern works on text too.

for (const ch of "hey") console.log(ch);
h
e
y
stages.p: Write letters(word) that counts each letter in word, ignoring capitals.
stages.h: Lowercase the word first, then tally each ch.

stages.l:
To find the most common, loop over the tally and keep the best so far.

let best = null;
for (const [k, v] of Object.entries({ a: 2, b: 5 })) {
  if (best === null || v > best[1]) best = [k, v];
}
console.log(best);
["b", 5]
stages.p: Write winner(count) that returns the key with the biggest number. If two tie, the one that comes first wins. If the object is empty, return null.
stages.h: Loop over Object.entries(count), keeping the best key and value. Use >, not >=, so the first one keeps a tie.

stages.l:
Now put it all together: split text into words, tally them, pick the winner.

console.log("the cat the end".split(" "));
["the", "cat", "the", "end"]
stages.p: Write topWord(text) that returns the word used most often (lowercased). Words are separated by single spaces. Ties go to the word seen first.
stages.h: Lowercase, split on " ", tally into an object, then find the key with the biggest count using >.
